issues.legal_issue: Buildings erected bona fide on another’s land with the landowner’s permission do not vest in the landowner merely because they are attached to the soil.
material_facts: The land belonged to the State.
With the State’s permission, a family member used joint-family funds to construct and manage a dharmasala, temple and shops on the land.
The buildings were not shown to have been transferred to the State.
issues.conclusion: The State did not acquire ownership of the buildings merely because they stood on State-owned land.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim that what is attached to the soil goes with the soil is not an absolute rule of law in India. A person who bona fide constructs buildings on another’s land with permission is not thereby a trespasser, and the buildings do not automatically vest in the landowner. The Court relied on Thakoor Chunder Parmanick v. Ramdhone Bhuttacharjee, Lala Beni Ram v. Kundan Lall, and Narayan Das Khettry v. Jatindranath.

predicates.construction_on_another_persons_land: The construction was erected on land belonging to someone other than the person who arranged or funded it.
predicates.bona_fide_construction: The construction was made bona fide rather than as a trespass.

issues.definition: When a bona fide construction is made on another person’s land with that person’s permission, the buildings do not automatically vest in the landowner.

issues.legal_issue: The State cannot dispossess a person in bona fide possession by executive action without authority of law, even where the person’s precise rights or trustee status are disputed.
material_facts: The family members continued managing and possessing the buildings after the original manager died.
The State’s officials used force to dispossess them from part of the dharmasala and handed its management and possession to the municipality.
The State did not establish legal authority for the executive dispossession.
The State argued that the family members were trespassers or trustees, but the Court found that neither characterization permitted removal by executive fiat.
issues.conclusion: The executive dispossession violated the petitioners’ fundamental rights; the orders were quashed and the respondents were restrained from interfering with their management of the properties.
issues.legal_principle: The State and its executive officers may not interfere with another’s rights without a specific rule of law authorising their acts. Even a trustee of a public trust can be removed only through procedure known to law; section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides a route for proceedings concerning a public trust. The Court relied on Wazir Chand v. The State of Himachal Pradesh and Ram Prasad Narayan Sahi v. The State of Bihar, and referred to Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. It did not decide the precise rights arising from the original permission or whether it created a lease or licence under section 60(b) of the Easements Act, 1882.

rule.if: fundamental_rights_writ and bona_fide_possession and executive_dispossession and not lawful_authority_for_dispossession

predicates.fundamental_rights_writ: The proceeding seeks constitutional relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.bona_fide_possession: The claimant was bona fide in possession of the property.
predicates.executive_dispossession: Government officials dispossessed the claimant by executive action.
predicates.lawful_authority_for_dispossession: A law or lawful process authorised the dispossession.

issues.definition: In a fundamental-rights proceeding, executive action that dispossesses a bona fide possessor without lawful authority is unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: Disputed questions of fact or title do not prevent constitutional writ relief when the admitted facts establish bona fide possession and unlawful dispossession, and resolving those disputes is unnecessary to decide the claim.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief under Article 32 after officials forcibly dispossessed them and transferred possession to the municipality.
The High Court had declined relief because the matter involved disputed questions of fact.
The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to determine the precise rights arising from the original permission or to resolve the disputed questions of fact and title.
The admitted facts established that the petitioners were bona fide in possession and had been removed without authority of law.
issues.conclusion: The factual and title disputes did not bar relief; the petitioners could obtain constitutional relief on the admitted facts.
issues.legal_principle: A writ proceeding need not determine disputed facts or precise title where the admitted facts suffice to establish the infringement of a fundamental right. The Court distinguished the objection based on Sohan Lal v. The Union of India because it was unnecessary to determine title or other disputed questions to grant relief.

rule.if: article_32_writ_proceeding and bona_fide_possession_established and unlawful_dispossession_established and disputed_title_unnecessary_to_resolve

predicates.article_32_writ_proceeding: The proceeding is a constitutional writ petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.bona_fide_possession_established: The admitted facts establish the claimant’s bona fide possession.
predicates.unlawful_dispossession_established: The admitted facts establish that the claimant was dispossessed without lawful authority.
predicates.disputed_title_unnecessary_to_resolve: The court can decide the claim without resolving disputed title or other disputed facts.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ proceeding establishes bona fide possession and unlawful dispossession on admitted facts, unresolved factual or title disputes do not bar relief if they need not be resolved.
